newsitem.title: USA: Shiva still aiming for FY98 EPS of $1.06.
newsitem.headline: Shiva still aiming for FY98 EPS of $1.06.

text.p: Shiva Corp Chief Financial Officer Cynthia Deysher said the company remains confident it can meet the Wall Street earnings consensus of $1.06 per share for fiscal 1998, despite a near-term earnings shortfall.

In addition, the Shiva executive said she expected earnings for the current quarter ending in March to be higher than the $0.05 to $0.07 per share the company has said it expects to report for its fourth quarter ended Dec. 28, 1996.
In a phone interview, Deysher said she expected revenues to fall but profit margins based on renegotiated terms of its strategic alliance with Northern Telecom Ltd to rise.
Shiva announced after the market close on Tuesday that it expected earnings for the recently ended fourth quarter of $0.05 to $0.07 a share, well below the consensus of $0.21.

Repeating comments she made in a call with analysts Tuesday evening, Deysher said that, "We indicated that we should be able to do better on earnings per share in Q1 than we did in Q4." Q1 refers to the first quarter ending in March.
"Our business plans are consistent with yesterday's street estimates, which were at $1.06 per share," Deysher added, referring to the current fiscal year ending January 3, 1998.
The comments did little to shore up Shiva on Wall Street.

Shares of the Bedford, Mass. maker of remote access networking equipment lost more than 45 percent of their value Wednesday morning. The stock rocketed to the top of the Nasdaq most actives with 9.5 million shares traded by mid-morning.
Analysts slashed earnings estimates and downgraded their stock ratings. According to First Call, of nine analysts who follow Shiva, five had cut numbers and or ratings.

The consensus rating fell to "barely above neutral" from "fairly bullish," according to First Call spokesman Chuck Hill. Of the five analysts who revised estimates, the new consensus for fiscal 1998 was $0.85 versus $1.07 previously.

Deysher said she told analysts to expect lower revenues as a result of its revised strategic alliance with Northern Telecom. She said NorTel would assume the costs of manufacturing products resulting from the alliance.
"We felt it would be more profitable because we are moving to a royalty arrangement" with Nortel, Deysher said, Shiva will be paid a percentage of sales rather than for each product it builds.
Late Tuesday, Deysher said the renegotiated pact with Northern Telecom was a response to a decline in revenues and earnings during the recently ended fourth quarter.

She blamed the shortfall in revenues on U.S. sales weakness, especially in its LAN Rover business, its most mature line of network products, and International Business Machines Corp's decision to delay an order in the quarter.

Deysher said the the company planned a series of measures including a reorganziation of its sales force into teams focused on its four core markets: corporate, enterprise, Internet service providers and telephone carriers.
In a statement on Tuesday announcing the expected earnings decline, the company had said it expected total revenue for the quarter ending December 28, 1996 to be about $48 to $50 million.
That range would represent a sequential decline from the $57.1 million in revenues reported in Shiva's third quarter ended in September.
